subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Adrenaline raises blood glucose, complementing glucagon, by:
options: Stimulating glycogenesis in muscle
Activating glycogenolysis via a second-messenger (cAMP) cascade in liver and muscle
Inhibiting respiration
Increasing insulin secretion
questions.explain: Adrenaline binds receptors that activate adenylate cyclase, raising cAMP to trigger glycogen breakdown and release of glucose.

questions.q: In a relaxed muscle, the myosin-binding sites on actin are blocked by:
options: ATP molecules
Myosin heads
Tropomyosin held in place by troponin
Calcium ions
questions.explain: At rest, tropomyosin covers the binding sites on actin, with troponin holding it there until calcium ions arrive.

questions.q: The cells lining the proximal convoluted tubule have many mitochondria and microvilli because they:
options: Carry out a large amount of active reabsorption requiring ATP and surface area
Secrete ADH into the filtrate
Filter the blood under high pressure
Produce urine of variable concentration
questions.explain: Reabsorbing most of the glucose, ions and water demands abundant ATP (mitochondria) and a large absorbing surface (microvilli).

questions.q: Glucagon raises blood glucose principally by stimulating:
options: Insulin secretion from beta cells
Glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver
Glycogenesis and glucose uptake
The conversion of glucose to fat
questions.explain: Glucagon promotes breakdown of glycogen (glycogenolysis) and synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources (gluconeogenesis) in the liver.

questions.q: After acetylcholine has acted on the postsynaptic membrane, it is broken down by acetylcholinesterase. The importance of this is to:
options: Provide energy for the next impulse
Increase the size of the next action potential
Prevent continuous stimulation so the synapse can respond to new impulses
Open more calcium channels
questions.explain: Hydrolysing acetylcholine stops prolonged depolarisation, allowing the receptors to reset and the products to be recycled.

questions.q: At a synapse, transmission is unidirectional because:
options: Calcium ions only enter the postsynaptic neurone
Acetylcholinesterase is found only presynaptically
Neurotransmitter receptors are only on the postsynaptic membrane and vesicles only on the presynaptic side
The synaptic cleft is too wide for diffusion
questions.explain: Vesicles releasing neurotransmitter are confined to the presynaptic neurone and receptors to the postsynaptic membrane, so signals pass one way.

questions.q: At a cholinergic synapse, the arrival of an action potential at the presynaptic membrane triggers:
options: Reuptake of acetylcholine
Influx of potassium ions
Opening of voltage-gated calcium channels, causing vesicles to fuse and release acetylcholine
Direct flow of current across the cleft
questions.explain: Depolarisation opens Ca2+ channels; calcium influx causes synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter by exocytosis.

questions.q: In the sliding filament theory, muscle contraction shortens the sarcomere because:
options: Myosin heads form cross-bridges and pull the actin filaments past the myosin toward the centre
Calcium ions are pumped out of the sarcoplasm
The actin and myosin filaments themselves shorten
The H zone widens as filaments slide apart
questions.explain: Myosin heads bind actin and, powered by ATP, pull the thin filaments inward so the sarcomere shortens while filament lengths stay the same.

questions.q: In the proximal convoluted tubule, glucose is reabsorbed by:
options: Pinocytosis of the filtrate
Co-transport with sodium ions across the apical membrane
Simple diffusion through the basement membrane
Osmosis following the water
questions.explain: Glucose is reabsorbed by sodium-glucose co-transport, the Na+ gradient being maintained by Na+/K+ pumps on the basolateral membrane.

questions.q: The counter-current multiplier in the loop of Henle works because:
options: The ascending limb is permeable to water but not ions
The descending limb actively pumps in water
Both limbs are equally permeable to water and ions
The ascending limb actively pumps out sodium ions, creating a high solute concentration (low water potential) in the medulla
questions.explain: Active removal of Na+ from the impermeable-to-water ascending limb builds a medullary solute gradient that draws water out of the descending limb and collecting duct.

questions.q: During the cross-bridge cycle, the binding of ATP to the myosin head causes it to:
options: Bind more tightly to actin
Detach from the actin filament
Bend and perform the power stroke
Release calcium ions
questions.explain: ATP binding to the myosin head breaks the cross-bridge, detaching it from actin so the cycle can repeat.

questions.q: Negative feedback in homeostasis acts to:
options: Amplify a deviation from the set point
Maintain a constant rate of change
Switch off all hormone secretion permanently
Reverse a change and return a factor toward its set point
questions.explain: Negative feedback detects a deviation and triggers responses that oppose it, restoring the internal environment toward the set point.

questions.q: An action potential is described as 'all-or-nothing'. This means:
options: The frequency of impulses cannot change
Once threshold is reached the action potential is always the same size regardless of stimulus strength
Larger stimuli produce larger action potentials
Sub-threshold stimuli produce small action potentials
questions.explain: Provided threshold is reached, an action potential of fixed magnitude is generated; stronger stimuli increase frequency, not size.

questions.q: Saltatory conduction in myelinated neurones speeds transmission because:
options: Myelin actively pumps sodium along the axon
The axon diameter is reduced by the myelin
The action potential jumps between nodes of Ranvier where depolarisation occurs
Myelin increases the membrane's permeability to sodium
questions.explain: Depolarisation only occurs at the gaps (nodes of Ranvier), so the impulse appears to jump from node to node, greatly increasing speed.

questions.q: How is the magnitude (intensity) of a stimulus conveyed to the central nervous system?
options: By the duration of the resting potential
By the size of each action potential
By the frequency of action potentials and the number of neurones firing
By the speed of the action potential
questions.explain: Because action potentials are all-or-nothing, a stronger stimulus is signalled by a higher firing frequency and recruitment of more neurones.

questions.q: Why does positive feedback rarely operate in mammalian homeostasis?
options: It cannot involve hormones
It amplifies a deviation away from the normal level, which is usually harmful
It uses too little energy to be effective
It returns a factor to its set point too quickly
questions.explain: Positive feedback drives a factor further from normal, so it is unsuitable for stabilising the internal environment except in special cases like childbirth.

questions.q: When the body overheats, heat loss is increased by:
options: Vasodilation of skin arterioles and increased sweating
Constriction of skin arterioles
Raising of body hairs
Shivering of skeletal muscle
questions.explain: Vasodilation brings more warm blood to the skin surface and sweating removes heat by evaporation, both increasing heat loss.

questions.q: The resting potential of a neurone (about -70 mV) is maintained by:
options: The sodium-potassium pump (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in) and the membrane's greater permeability to K+
Voltage-gated sodium channels being open
Equal diffusion of sodium and potassium ions
Continuous influx of sodium ions
questions.explain: The Na+/K+ pump plus relatively high K+ permeability (and large anions inside) make the inside negative relative to the outside.

questions.q: On a cold day, the body conserves heat by:
options: Relaxation of erector pili muscles
Vasodilation of skin arterioles
Increased sweating
Vasoconstriction of skin arterioles, reducing blood flow to the surface
questions.explain: Vasoconstriction reduces blood flow near the skin surface, decreasing heat loss by radiation.

questions.q: In a healthy person, beta cells of the islets of Langerhans detect a rise in blood glucose when:
options: Glucagon binds to their surface receptors
Glucose entering the cell increases ATP, closing potassium channels and triggering insulin release
Glycogen is broken down in the liver
Adrenaline is secreted by the adrenal glands
questions.explain: Increased glucose uptake raises ATP, closing K+ channels; the resulting depolarisation opens Ca2+ channels and triggers insulin secretion by exocytosis.

questions.q: The role of calcium ions in muscle contraction is to:
options: Break the cross-bridges between actin and myosin
Bind to troponin, moving tropomyosin to expose the myosin-binding sites on actin
Resynthesise ATP from ADP
Provide the energy for the power stroke
questions.explain: Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin, shifting tropomyosin to uncover actin binding sites so cross-bridges can form.

questions.q: During the refractory period immediately after an action potential, a second impulse cannot be generated because:
options: The sodium channels are inactivated and the membrane is recovering its resting state
Calcium ions block the axon
The potassium channels are permanently open
Myelin temporarily disappears
questions.explain: Inactivated Na+ channels and ongoing repolarisation mean the membrane cannot fire again, ensuring discrete, one-way impulses.

questions.q: The repolarisation phase of an action potential is brought about by:
options: Potassium channels opening so K+ diffuses out of the axon
The sodium-potassium pump alone
Sodium channels opening
Calcium ions entering the axon
questions.explain: Voltage-gated K+ channels open and K+ leaves the axon, restoring the negative internal potential (repolarisation).

questions.q: When the water potential of the blood falls, ADH is released and causes:
options: Increased filtration at the glomerulus
The loop of Henle to pump out more sodium
Less water to be reabsorbed, producing dilute urine
More aquaporins to be inserted into the collecting duct, increasing water reabsorption
questions.explain: ADH makes the collecting duct walls more permeable by inserting aquaporins, so more water is reabsorbed and concentrated urine is produced.

questions.q: In the eye, the iris controls the amount of light reaching the retina. In bright light, the:
options: Circular muscles contract to constrict the pupil
Both sets of muscles relax
Pupil dilates to admit more light
Radial muscles contract to widen the pupil
questions.explain: Bright light triggers a reflex in which the circular muscles of the iris contract, narrowing the pupil to protect the retina.

questions.q: In the second messenger model of glucagon action, the binding of glucagon to its receptor leads to:
options: Activation of adenylate cyclase, raising cyclic AMP, which activates protein kinase A
Direct entry of glucagon into the cell to activate enzymes
Insulin being released by exocytosis
Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels
questions.explain: Glucagon activates adenylate cyclase, producing cAMP as a second messenger that activates protein kinase A to trigger glycogenolysis.

questions.q: In a control system, a receptor, a coordinator and an effector act in sequence. The coordinator's role is to:
options: Set a new value for the factor being controlled
Bring about the corrective response
Receive information from receptors and instruct effectors to respond
Detect the change in the environment
questions.explain: The coordinator (e.g. brain or endocrine gland) processes input from receptors and signals effectors to produce an appropriate response.

questions.q: Depolarisation during an action potential is caused by:
options: Potassium ions diffusing out of the axon
The sodium-potassium pump reversing direction
Chloride ions entering the axon
Voltage-gated sodium channels opening and Na+ flooding into the axon
questions.explain: At threshold, voltage-gated Na+ channels open and Na+ rushes in, making the inside positive (depolarisation).

questions.q: Type 1 diabetes differs from type 2 in that:
options: Type 1 results from autoimmune destruction of beta cells so little or no insulin is produced
Type 1 has a later onset and is linked to obesity
Type 1 is caused by target cells losing responsiveness to insulin
Type 1 is usually treated by diet and exercise alone
questions.explain: In type 1 the immune system destroys insulin-secreting beta cells, whereas type 2 involves reduced insulin sensitivity of target cells.

questions.q: When blood glucose rises after a meal, insulin lowers it by:
options: Converting amino acids and glycerol into glucose
Stimulating glycogenolysis in the liver
Increasing the uptake of glucose by cells and promoting glycogenesis
Inhibiting respiration in muscle cells
questions.explain: Insulin raises glucose uptake (via more GLUT4 channels) and promotes glycogenesis, converting glucose to glycogen for storage.
